newsitem.title: USA: Dollar rallies after steep Swiss rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Dollar rallies after steep Swiss rate cut.

text.p: The dollar climbed against major currencies Thursday after a surprisingly large cut in Swiss interest rates hurt the Swiss franc and the German mark, traders and analysts said.
Lower rates in Switzerland make the dollar more attractive by enhancing the relative value of dollar-denominated assets.

The Swiss National Bank, Switzerland's central bank, cut its discount rate to an 18-year low at 1.0 percent from 1.5 percent in a bid to spur its sluggish economy. Investors promptly sold Swiss francs and German marks for dollars.

"People understood Switzerland had to do something to get its economy going. I don't think they were quite ready to see such a large reduction in rates," said Lisa Finstrom, currency analyst at Smith Barney.

The dollar late Thursday rose to 1.2530 Swiss francs from 1.2415 late on Wednesday and to 1.5230 German marks from 1.5170. Against the Japanese yen, the dollar rose to 110.63 from 110.47. The British pound stood unchanged at $1.5613. The dollar rose to Canadian $1.3675 from C$1.3663.
The dollar's rally against the Swiss franc also hurt the mark, with investors also expecting lower German interest rates in coming months.
"People that had been flocking to the Swiss franc got hurt a bit and the higher dollar puts pressure on the mark," said Gabriel Grippo, chief currency dealer at Credit Agricole.

The Italian lira saw solid buying for a second straight day, bolstered by official Italian predictions that Italy would slash its budget deficit in 1997 and qualify for a proposed single European currency.
The lira remained near its strongest level in two years, reached Wednesday, below 1000 to the mark. The selling of marks for lira also bolstered the dollar against the mark, dealers said.
"There was more talk about Italy doing well. That should continue to put pressure on the mark and put legs under the dollar," Grippo said.
Much of the dollar's rally occurred in Asian and European trading. As markets closed in Europe, many investors sold off dollars to take profits, thus limiting further gains.
But an afternoon report that a top Japanese economic official called the United States the best place for Japanese investment helped the dollar edge to a session high against the yen.

Meanwhile, influential economist Fred Bergsten, director of the Institute for International Economics, told reporters in Washington that Japanese officials were seeking to weaken the yen to lower the cost of Japanese exports.
"The dollar has to play some catch-up against the yen," said Grippo. "I think tomorrow we should take out 111 (yen) and test 111.50."
The dollar's 1996 high is 111.19 yen reached on July 8.
Investors appear to have already forgotten their disappointment at Federal Reserve officials' decision not to raise interest rates at a policy-making meeting on Tuesday.

A report of a surprising drop of 3.1 percent in durable goods orders in August eased many investors' fears that the economy might overheat, feeding inflation. That encouraged a sharp rally in Treasury bond prices and boosted the dollar, dealers said.

"There was a little nervousness about how prudent that Fed decision will prove to be, but now there's a perception that our long-term interest rates aren't looking so fearful," Smith Barney's Finstrom said.
